__________

The debate is framed wrong.
SEO, AEO, GEO, SXO and AIO are not five rival strategies.
They are five layers of the same discovery system.

SEO builds the foundation.
→ Make pages crawlable, technically sound and easy to understand.
→ Target real search intent with useful content and internal links.
→ Without this base, every newer acronym has less to work with.

AEO earns the direct answer.
→ Structure clear responses for snippets, FAQs and voice results.
→ Use schema where it helps machines interpret the page.
→ If the answer is buried, zero-click visibility goes elsewhere.

GEO earns the citation.
→ Create authoritative passages that ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity can reference.
→ Strengthen entities, E-E-A-T signals and topical depth.
→ Check whether AI answers mention your brand, not just your category.

SXO turns attention into action.
→ Improve speed, clarity, navigation and calls to action.
→ Track whether visitors engage, convert or leave confused.
→ Ranking without a useful experience produces traffic, not momentum.

AIO prepares content for AI consumption.
→ Use semantic structure, clean code and reusable content blocks.
→ Make key claims easy to extract without losing context.
→ Design for people first, then make the meaning machine-readable.

The practical sequence matters.
1. Audit technical SEO and indexability.
2. Rewrite weak pages around one clear search intent.
3. Add concise answer blocks for high-value questions.
4. Test citations across ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity.
5. Fix the experience between landing page and next action.

Do not assign every acronym to a separate team.
Create one shared scorecard for visibility, answers, citations, experience and reuse.
Review it monthly against the pages that matter most.

The diagnostic is simple.
❌ Rankings but no clicks: revisit the result and intent.
❌ Clicks but no action: fix SXO friction.
❌ Strong pages but no AI mentions: improve GEO evidence and entity clarity.
❌ Useful content but poor extraction: strengthen AEO and AIO structure.

The winning model is additive.
SEO gets you found.
AEO gets you selected.
GEO gets you cited.
SXO gets users moving.
AIO keeps the content useful in an AI-first interface.

Treat the five layers as one operating system.
The teams that connect them will compound every improvement.
The teams that chase acronyms will keep rebuilding the same foundation.

Which layer would your team need to audit first?

Prompt engineering is dead

According to Nvidia's co-founder and the Head of Claude Code

We should write in loops and not prompts.

A prompt gives you one answer.

A loop gives you a system that can repeat the work, check the result, fix mistakes, and stop only when the goal is met.

That is the shift.

The future is not about asking AI better questions.

It is about designing better instructions for how AI should work through a task.

A good loop has 7 parts:

1. Goal: What should be achieved.
2. Work Source: Where the task comes from.
3. Rules: How the AI should behave.
4. Process: The steps it should follow.
5. Verification Checklist: How it checks the work.
6. Stop Condition: When the loop should end.
7. Escalation: When the AI should ask for human review.

This is how AI becomes more useful.

You stop babysitting every single response.
You give it a structure.
You give it a checklist.
You give it a stopping point.

That is how you move from prompting to building systems.

Stop wasting energy on the wrong people.

Focus on the ones who WANT to grow.

After coaching 650+ CEOs, I keep seeing the same pattern.

The leaders with the strongest teams refuse to manage everyone the same way. They diagnose each person individually and adjust their approach to fit.

One of the simplest tools for this is the Skill/Will Matrix, created by Max Landsberg.

It plots every team member on two axes: skill (their ability and experience) and will (their motivation and drive).

The result is four very different types of people, each needing a very different leadership response.

🟡 Top Performers sit in the high-skill, high-will quadrant. They deliver, they push themselves, and they raise the bar for everyone around them.

These are the people you build the future of the company around. Give them ownership. Ask for their input. Raise expectations over time. Recognize them often.

The mistake is overloading them just because they can handle it. Stretch them, but invest in them too.

🟢 High Potentials have the will but not yet the skill. They are eager, hungry, and ready to grow. They just need reps.

Coach them. Break their work into small wins. Celebrate progress over perfection. Pair them with a mentor. These are your future Top Performers if you develop them well.

🔵 Disengaged Experts are the trickiest group. They have the skill, but the motivation has gone. They might be bored, burnt out, or quietly outgrowing the role.

Ask what's behind the disconnect. Reconnect them to the mission. Adjust their goals or responsibilities. Set a clear timeline for change. If nothing changes, you have your answer.

🔴 Low Performers drain energy from the rest of the team. They lack the skill and the drive to build it.

Set clear expectations, give one chance to improve, and exit respectfully if nothing changes. Keeping them in place tells everyone else that your standards are negotiable.

People will not always fit neatly into one box, and skill and will both shift over time.

The point of the matrix is to lead each person according to where they are right now. That's where your energy compounds.

I dreaded negotiations early in my career.

Then I realized:

You don’t have to be confrontational
to be a strong negotiator.

All it takes is using the right frameworks.

Here are 5 proven approaches to negotiate
every deal more effectively:

🤝 The 4 Phases Framework
(h/t: Roy Lewicki)

Great negotiators don’t jump straight to bargaining. 
They follow a structured process:

• Preparation (lay the groundwork)
• Information Exchange (build mutual understanding)
• Bargaining (explore potential solutions)
• Commitment (secure the agreement)

💪 The BATNA Strategy
(h/t: Roger Fisher & William Ury)

Your power in any negotiation comes from knowing 
your Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement (BATNA).

It’s your safety net, your source of confidence. 
Always define it before you start.

🎯 The Negotiation Matrix
(h/t: Lewicki & Hiam)

Different situations call for different strategies:

• High stakes? Compete.
• Building a long-term relationship? Collaborate.
• Minor issue? Avoidance might be best.
• The relationship is too critical? Accommodate.
• Both matter equally? Compromise.

🤔 The Harvard Principled Negotiation Method
(h/t: Fisher, Ury & Patton)

This is a game-changer:
Focus on interests, not positions.

Instead of asking what they want, ask why they want it.

That’s where real value creation happens.

🎯 The ZOPA Framework
(h/t: Fisher & Ury)

The Zone of Possible Agreement (ZOPA) is where deals get made.

Understanding both sides’ limits helps you identify common ground. 

Everything else? It's just noise.

Key takeaway:

The best deals happen when both sides feel heard.

And the most successful negotiators aren’t the most aggressive.

They’re simply the most prepared.

Most companies are bleeding cash in 4 spots.

Every dollar leaving your business falls into one of these buckets:

OPERATIONS (OpEx) - The Daily Bleed
↳ Your rent, salaries, software subscriptions

ASSETS (CapEx) - The Big Bets
↳ That $50K machine, new warehouse, custom software
↳ Spend once, use for years
↳ Get it wrong? You're stuck with expensive mistakes

• RevEx: $3 per cup sold (beans, cup, lid)

• RevEx: $20 per customer (payment fees, onboarding)
• FinEx: $2K/month (venture debt interest)

Most founders lump all expenses together.
Then wonder why they can't scale.

OpEx → Find your true burn rate
CapEx → Time investments perfectly
RevEx → Price products profitably
FinEx → Optimize capital structure

✓ High OpEx? You're not scalable yet
✓ No CapEx? You're not building moats
✓ Rising RevEx? Your unit economics are broken
✓ Climbing FinEx? You're overleveraged

Common traps:

❌ Treating CapEx like OpEx (and vice versa)
❌ Ignoring RevEx when setting prices
❌ Letting FinEx compound silently
❌ Not tracking any of them separately

Watch what happens when you finally see where your money really goes.

Your future self will thank you.

I used to wear 14-hour days like a badge of honor.

I thought rest was what you did after the work was done.

It took years to learn that rest is part of the work.

Your body needs seven different types of breaks.

Each one has a specific window where it works best.

Skip them and the hours keep going but the output drops.

7 breaks that protect your performance:

1/ THE MICRO-REST
→ Focus fades after 60 to 90 minutes of deep work
→ That dip is a signal, not a failure
→ Step away before it hits. Look at the horizon. Walk for 10 to 20 minutes

2/ THE BREATHING RESET
→ When stress spikes mid-task, you may not have 10 minutes
→ One breathing cycle takes about 10 seconds
→ Long inhale through the nose, short second inhale, long exhale

3/ THE POWER BREAK
→ The afternoon slump is real and predictable
→ A 10 to 20 minute nap or eyes-closed rest gives you a second wind
→ Finish well before evening so night sleep stays intact

4/ THE LUNCH BREAK
→ Midday is your best shot at a true reset
→ Eat away from your desk, leave your phone behind
→ Skip the work talk for 30 to 60 minutes

5/ THE SHUTDOWN RITUAL
→ A workday without a clear ending never really ends
→ Signal "work is over" the same way each day
→ Phone away for the evening. Takes 10 to 15 minutes

6/ THE WEEKEND RECOVERY
→ Not all time off restores you
→ Real recovery means stepping fully out of work mode
→ Spend time in nature, build a skill, take one full day off screens

7/ THE STRATEGIC VACATION
→ Recovery follows a curve. It peaks around day 7, then fades
→ Frequent planned breaks beat one long trip you save up for
→ Take one week off every three months. Book it non-refundable

Three out of four people experience burnout at work.

Most of them think the answer is pushing through.

The answer is better breaks, taken on purpose.

A Stanford study tracked 30,000 adults over eight years.

People under high stress had a 43% higher risk of dying.

But only if they believed stress was harmful.

The ones who saw stress as useful? No increased risk at all.

Same pressure. Different response. Different outcome.

That finding changed how Dr. Christian Poensgen and I think about performance.

The goal was never to remove stress. Stress is a fact of life.

Instead, you learn to stop the good kind from tipping into the bad.

8 ways to make that shift:

1/ ACUTE VS. CHRONIC STRESS
→ Acute stress sharpens focus and settles fast
→ Chronic stress scatters it and stays on
→ The difference is duration and recovery

2/ THE STRESS-IS-ENHANCING MINDSET (h/t Alia Crum)
→ Notice the stress, welcome it, then channel it
→ Your beliefs about stress actually change its biology

3/ THE SYNERGISTIC MINDSET (h/t David Yeager)
→ Growth mindset alone stalls at the first failure
→ Pair it with a stress-is-fuel mindset and both compound

4/ STRESS VS. ANXIETY
→ Stress has a clear trigger and a built-in off-ramp
→ Anxiety is diffuse, future-focused, and lingers without resolution

5/ SET STRESS GOALS (h/t Kelly McGonigal)
→ Avoiding stress shrinks your life
→ Pick 3 ambitious goals a year that are hard on purpose

6/ MINE YOUR PAST WINS
→ 82% of adults draw on past wins to face new stress
→ Spend 15 minutes writing about a win you had to fight for

7/ OSCILLATE, DON'T FLATLINE (h/t Loehr & Schwartz)
→ Constant output climbs, then collapses
→ Sprint and recover. That's what sustainable performance looks like

8/ TRACK YOUR HRV
→ Heart rate variability measures your stress-rest flexibility
→ High HRV shifts gears cleanly. Low HRV means you're stuck in high gear

items.content:
Never regret being a kind leader.

The way you treat people comes back multiplied.

I used to wonder if kindness was costing me.

If being generous with my time, my patience, my belief in people was making me look weak.

I questioned it. Then something happened.

A former team member called me three years later. She said one conversation I'd had with her changed how she led her own team.

I barely remembered it. But she never forgot.

That's the thing about kindness in leadership. You rarely see the return in real time. But it compounds.

Let me be clear:

Kindness isn't weakness.
Kindness isn't letting things slide.
Kindness isn't avoiding tough calls.

It's choosing respect when frustration would be easier.
It's choosing patience when pressure says react.
It's choosing people over ego.

6 ways it comes back multiplied:

1. The person you believed in before they believed in themselves. They become your biggest advocate years later.

2. The grace you gave during someone's worst season. They remember. And they pay it forward to others.

3. The honest feedback you delivered with dignity. They grew from it instead of resenting you.

4. The credit you gave publicly when no one required it. Loyalty built in seconds. Lasting for years.

5. The time you listened when you had every reason to rush. Trust deepened. Communication opened permanently.

6. The second chance you offered without making it a spectacle. They showed up differently. Permanently.

People remember the moment you treated them like they mattered.

You will never lose by being kind.

You might lose people who don't value it. But those aren't your people.

The ones who stay build something remarkable with you.

Never apologize for leading with kindness. It's not soft. It's rare.

And it's exactly what people remember.

I spent 15 years researching how top performers actually run their days.

One number kept surfacing.

90.

It shows up in 7 places, from your next 90 minutes to your next 90 days.

✅ How long you stay sharp before focus drops.
✅ How your body rebuilds while you sleep.
✅ How long a wave of emotion takes to pass.

7 common places you find 90 in your life:

90 Minutes of Deep Focus
↳ Do your most important work in one focused block
↳ Then stop. Your brain needs the reset

A Break Every 90 Minutes
↳ Step away for 5–20 minutes between blocks
↳ Walk, breathe, deep rest. Come back sharper

90 Minutes of Deep Sleep
↳ Your body rebuilds itself in the first half of the night
↳ Protect those minutes. They're when recovery happens

90 Minutes of REM Sleep
↳ Your brain processes emotions in the second half
↳ 7.5 hours of sleep helps you get the full cycle

90 Minutes Screen-Free Before Bed
↳ No phone for the last 90 minutes of your day
↳ Let your brain wind down without digital noise

90 Seconds to Reset Your Emotions
↳ When a strong feeling hits, pause and breathe slowly
↳ 90 seconds is all it takes for the wave to pass

Every 90 Days, Reset Your Priorities
↳ Once a quarter, block 1 hour
↳ Pick your top 3 goals for the next 90 days

When you work with your natural rhythms, you accomplish more and feel better doing it.

You spend every day running on 90 whether you notice it or not. Start noticing.

items.content:
Teams fall apart for one reason.

(Every CEO needs to know this)

Missing layers.

Team performance has 4 layers. And they must be built from the bottom up.

Layer 1: Trust. This is the foundation everything else sits on. Psychological safety, vulnerability, consistency, respect, honesty, follow-through.

Layer 2: Clarity. Everyone knows what winning looks like. Defined roles, shared goals, expectations, KPIs, priorities, boundaries.

Layer 3: Accountability. People own their outcomes. No hiding. No excuses. Scorecards, weekly check-ins, honest feedback, consequences, recognition, clear ownership.

Layer 4: Results. Performance becomes the default, not the exception. Execution speed, innovation, growth, quality, retention.

Most leaders think they just need to push harder. Demand more from their people. Be more direct.

But if you haven’t build trust, every layer above it crumbles.

I see this pattern constantly. Leaders push for results while their teams lack the safety to speak up. The clarity to align. The ownership to deliver.

If your team is underperforming, don't look at the top layer. Look at the bottom one.
